parity_notes: TS-PARITY FIRST (the task's step 2): TS DOES hold its auth lock across the SAME token fetch - auth-storage.ts refreshOAuthTokenWithLock runs `await getOAuthApiKey(providerId, oauthCreds)` INSIDE storage.withLockAsync (proper-lockfile.lock retries 10x100-10000ms stale 30000, readFileSync -> await fn -> writeFileAtomicSync, release). The Rust port's refresh-under-with_lock is a FAITHFUL port. The candidate is therefore NOT a TS convergence but a deliberate, disclosed Rust-side lock-scope narrowing: TS's single-threaded runtime never observes in-process contention on the held lock; the threaded Rust engine serializes ALL same-process auth I/O behind the fetch (#2932's process_lock spans the whole with_lock), which the census shows as the concurrent reader queueing ~190ms behind the refresher. Frozen surfaces untouched: no session-JSONL/compaction/wire/prompt/TUI byte changed (the auth file protocol is byte-identical - the same with_lock read-modify-write arm; read results identical; every resolution outcome preserved including the failed-fetch path returning None, the unexpired fast path, and the Err-path reload-and-serve-stored shape). Cross-process divergence introduced and disclosed: TS serializes two processes' refreshes through the lockfile (the second blocks, sees fresh, never fetches); with the fetch outside the lock two processes may fetch concurrently - the in-lock re-check keeps the peer's fresher credential (this attempt writes nothing) so the document state converges identically, at the cost of a rare extra network call. In-process, the per-provider single-flight gate + its expiry re-check preserve TS's single-flight semantics exactly (a second caller joins the first flight and serves its fresh credential without spending a single-use refresh token).
